name: bloodhound
one_line: map Active Directory attack paths as a graph
plain: An Active Directory (AD) domain is a big web of users, groups, computers and permissions. BloodHound collects that data, draws it as a graph and answers: starting from this user, what is the shortest path to Domain Admin?

You use it in two steps. First a collector gathers data from the domain (SharpHound on Windows, bloodhound-python from Linux). Second you upload the zip into BloodHound and run queries or click through the graph.
It is used by defenders to find and cut dangerous paths, and by pen testers and CTF players in authorised labs. Use it only on domains you own or have permission to test.
when: Find who has admin on which machines.
Find the shortest path from a compromised user to Domain Admins.
Find dangerous permissions (GenericAll, WriteDacl, DCSync rights).
As a defender, measure and reduce attack paths.

examples.title: Collect from Linux (lab)
examples.explain: -u/-p are lab credentials, -d the domain, -ns the DNS server (usually the domain controller), -c All collects everything, --zip packs the JSON files for upload.

examples.title: Collect from Windows (lab)
examples.explain: SharpHound runs on a domain-joined host and writes a zip. Some environments detect and block it.

examples.title: Start and sign in
examples.explain: On Kali the legacy version needs Neo4j started and its password set once. Newer BloodHound Community Edition runs as a web service; follow its first-run instructions.

examples.title: Upload the data
examples.cmd: Upload Data (right side) > select the zip
examples.explain: The graph fills as the files are imported. Wait for the import to finish before querying.

examples.title: Run a pre-built query
examples.cmd: Analysis > Shortest Paths to Domain Admins
examples.explain: Draws the shortest chains of relationships from any account to the Domain Admins group. Click each edge for help on how to abuse or fix it.

examples.title: Mark what you own
examples.cmd: Right-click a user > Mark User as Owned
examples.explain: Owned accounts are the starting points. Then use 'Shortest Paths from Owned Principals'.

examples.title: Find Kerberoastable accounts
examples.explain: Service accounts with a service principal name can have their tickets requested and cracked offline.

examples.title: Find AS-REP roastable accounts
examples.explain: Accounts that do not require Kerberos pre-authentication leak crackable data.

examples.title: Look up one account
examples.cmd: Search box > type the name > click it
examples.explain: Shows its properties, group memberships, sessions and outbound control in the node panel.

examples.title: Write your own query
examples.cmd: Raw Query bar: MATCH p=shortestPath((u:User {name:'ALICE@CORP.LOCAL'})-[*1..]->(g:Group {name:'DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.LOCAL'})) RETURN p
examples.explain: The Cypher language lets you ask any question of the graph. This one is the shortest path from one user to Domain Admins.

options.plain: Pick a start and an end node; BloodHound draws a path.
Pre-built queries: Domain Admins, Shortest Paths to Domain Admins, Kerberoastable, AS-REP roastable, unconstrained delegation, high-value targets.
Properties, memberships, sessions, local admin rights for the selected node.

mistakes: Treating BloodHound as proof of vulnerability: it shows possible paths; confirm each step.
Collecting with -c All on a monitored network: it is noisy.
Forgetting DNS: bloodhound-python often needs -ns pointing to the domain controller.
Importing partial or old data and trusting an old graph.
Using it on a domain you do not own: it generates real queries and logs.

Run 'Shortest Paths to Domain Admins' and read the edge help for each step.
